summary: The Superconducting Quasiparticle-Amplifying Transmon (SQUAT) is a new sensor architecture for meV/THz detection based on a weakly charge-sensitive transmon ($E_J/E_C \sim 25$) directly coupled to a transmission line without an intermediate readout resonator. This first experimental demonstration validates the SQUAT design using aluminum-based prototypes on sapphire, achieving simultaneous readout of charge and parity signals with noise temperatures around 10.37 K and coherence times $T_1 \sim 50$–100 ns.
motivation: Superconducting qubits are inherently sensitive to quasiparticle poisoning from sub-meV energy depositions, but this sensitivity can be repurposed for direct detection of rare events such as dark-matter interactions and THz photons by monitoring parity-switching rates induced by quasiparticle tunneling across the Josephson junction.
method: The authors fabricated three-SQUAT chips using Al/AlOx/Al Dolan junctions on niobium-ground-plane sapphire substrates, characterized resonance properties via VNA transmission measurements ($f_0 \sim 7$–8.5 GHz, $2\chi_0 \sim 2$–10 MHz, $Q_r \sim 1000$), extracted $T_1$ and $T_2^*$ via pulsed sequences, and measured background parity-switching rates as a function of temperature, readout power, and environmental conditions.
result: Devices exhibited background parity-switching rates as low as 10–40 Hz (pulse-tube off) dominated by temperature-independent processes at millikelvin temperatures; gap asymmetry $\delta\Delta \approx 2$ GHz was extracted from thermal activation fits; readout fidelity reached 50% at 6 kHz bandwidth; simultaneous charge-parity detection was demonstrated when charge-dependent dispersion varied from $\chi = 0$ to $\chi_0$, with infrared shielding reducing switching rates by multiple orders of magnitude.
